messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rohan, a 36-year-old detective of South Asian descent, had always prided himself on being a rock for his loved ones. But behind closed doors, he struggled with demons that haunted him since childhood. Growing up, Rohan endured physical abuse at the hands of his caregiver, an experience that left an indelible mark on his psyche. As an adult, certain triggers transported Rohan back to those dark days. The sensation of a specific temperature on his skin would send shivers down his spine, making him feel like he was reliving the trauma all over again. He couldn't quite explain why, but sleeping alone or in unfamiliar places made him anxious, too - perhaps it was the feeling of vulnerability that came with not having someone to rely on for protection. Even the sound of doors opening or slamming would startle him, as if his body was constantly on high alert. These triggers reinforced Rohan's deepest fears: that he was a lousy coper, unable to handle the stressors of life. He felt like he didn't know himself anymore - the confident detective who solved crimes with ease had given way to a fragile individual who couldn't even manage his own emotions. And beneath it all, there was a nagging sense that something was fundamentally wrong with him as a person. As Rohan's self-doubt grew, so did his maladaptive strategies for coping. He began avoiding people, including his loving wife and colleagues, in an attempt to shield himself from further emotional pain. Staying up late into the night became a habit, too - by delaying sleep, Rohan felt like he was maintaining some semblance of control over his life. And going out? That seemed like an impossible task; what if something triggered another flashback or anxiety attack? But these avoidance behaviors only served to reinforce Rohan's negative self-image. By pushing people away, he convinced himself that he was indeed unworthy of love and connection. His late-night wakefulness led to fatigue, which further eroded his confidence in his ability to cope with the demands of his job. And by staying indoors, Rohan felt like a prisoner in his own home - another reminder that something was defective about him. As time passed, Rohan's negative appraisals began to sensitize him to even more triggers. The slightest noise would send him spiraling back into memories he'd rather forget. And the cycle continued: avoidance led to feelings of inadequacy, which in turn amplified his sensitivity to those triggers that haunted him most. It wasn't until Rohan's wife staged an intervention - expressing her deep concern for his well-being and their relationship - that he realized he needed help. The thought of losing the people he loved, coupled with the toll his symptoms were taking on his job performance, finally pushed Rohan to seek therapy. As he sat in the therapist's office, he couldn't shake off the feeling that this was a last-ditch effort to reclaim his life - and himself.
